en: Black's king finally collects the pawn. It will have cost him four tempi — and the game.
First pawn. Black's king is six files away: he will never get back.
Second pawn, and two connected pawns escorted by their king against a bare king. The decoy did everything: it never threatened to queen, it merely bought four tempi — exactly what was needed.

Rook and bishop versus rook is generally a draw — three courses in this catalogue teach how to hold it. Here is the exception Philidor analysed back in 1749: the defending king trapped on the back rank, FACING the attacking king, loses even against best defence. Only one of White's 23 moves wins here — and every step of the manoeuvre has a precise meaning.
Philidor's manoeuvre, move by move
The natural move that lets it all slip
The ONLY winning move out of 23 (tablebase-checked — everything else is a draw). The check forces Black's rook to interpose on e8, where it blocks its king's own escape square.
Building a mating threat with the bishop looks natural — and only DRAWS (verified: the position drops from won to drawn). Black's rook has an astonishing resource.

The heart of the idea: White's rook seizes the 7th rank and threatens mate from the side. Black's rook is in zugzwang — it cannot stay on e8 (it must meet Ra7-a8), so it has to leave the 8th rank and abandon its king.
The tablebase's toughest defence: the rook runs as far as it can, ready to harass from behind.
Black's rook must guard the c-file — otherwise Rb8+ followed by mate. It is now tied to a single file: exactly what White wanted.
First step of the bishop triangle (b3-e6-d5): the bishop leaves d5 while GAINING a tempo — from b3 it still eyes e6, preparing to return to d5 at the exact moment it most inconveniences Black's rook.

The triangle is complete: same position as before, but Black's rook has been pushed from c1 to d3 — a far worse square, as the sequel shows. Losing a tempo to hand the move back: the very weapon of triangulation in pawn endings.
Now that Black's rook no longer sits on c1, the black king is evicted from d8 — towards the side where White's rook awaits it.
The final net: the rook aims for a4, then a8. Against the threat of Be6+ followed by Rb8 mate, the defence is down to one-move resources.
Threatening Ra8 mate (the d5-bishop covers the b7 escape square). Black's rook has a single resource left: throwing itself at the bishop.
The desperado sacrifice — literally the tablebase's best defence: everything else gets mated faster.

What remains is king and rook versus king: the elementary mate, taught in its own course. Philidor's lesson ends here — remember the trio: the check forcing the interposition, the 7th rank, the bishop triangle.
The counterblow: a check AND a rook offer. Declining it forces White's king to give up d6, and all the pressure evaporates.
Stalemate! The black king has no square left (the d7-bishop covers c8 and e8, White's king covers the rest) and no piece to move. That is why only 1.Rf8+ wins: it never lets this counterplay arise.

A pawn down in a rook ending? Philidor showed in 1749 that the draw is PLAYED, in two steps: the rook bars the sixth rank, then — the moment the pawn steps onto it — swings behind for endless checks. The best-paying defence in chess.
The barrier, then the checks
The barrier holds by itself
The trade that loses everything
Grabbing the pawn too soon
The BARRIER: the rook camps on the very rank the white king must cross, and denies all of it. Until the pawn advances, there is NO way through.

“Trade rooks and breathe.” Look at the pawn ending BEFORE trading: the white king stands IN FRONT of his pawn — a textbook win for him (see “The Opposition”). Trading rooks is the LAST decision of a rook ending: after it, there is no defence left.
The only try: push the pawn to give the sixth rank back to the king. But that pawn just lost its last shadow — nothing will shelter the white king from checks now.
Chase the black king? He only needs two squares.
The PIVOT — all of Philidor lives in this move: the barrier's job done, the rook races to THE FAR END to strafe from behind. Not sooner, not later: exactly when the pawn touches the sixth rank.
Is the pawn free? No: it is BAIT. The white king covered it — the black rook just sold itself for a pawn.
And so it begins. Count the white king's shelters: there are none.
The rook checks from MAXIMUM range: eight ranks away, the king can never walk over to shoo it.
Perpetual. The white king may wander where he likes: with no shelter, every square is worth exactly one more check. The draw is a fact now, not a hope.
The king stays in touch with the promotion square — never further than the next rank.
And nothing better exists: the sixth rank stays sealed, the position repeats.
Back exactly where we started. That is the barrier's beauty: it demands NOTHING but patience.
All that remains is an opposition lesson — on the wrong side of it.
Rook for pawn. The rest is “The Rook Mate” course, played against you.

A pure pawn race: three tempi each, both pawns promote — a draw, says the count. Wrong: the black king stands on the long a8-h1 diagonal, the one connecting BOTH promotion squares. So White's queen is born with check, and devours the g2-pawn along that very diagonal a move later. Counting tempi is never enough: always look at what the new queen will see from its birth square.
Push, push, promote with check
One escorting tempo — and the check changes sides

The ONLY winning move out of eight (verified: four king moves draw, three lose). In a pure race every king tempo is a tempo stolen from the race — and the b5-king already does its whole job standing still: it covers c6, the square the black king would need to catch the pawn.
Escorting the pawn with the king: the right instinct in queen endings… and here, the mistake that throws the win away (verified: the position drops from won to drawn). The race waits for no one.
Black races too — the tablebase's best defence. Three tempi against three: on paper, nobody wins this race.

The promotion lands with CHECK — and the whole ending was decided right there, from the start: the black king stands on the long a8-h1 diagonal, the one linking the two promotion squares. Count the tempi, then ALWAYS check that geometry.

The king must answer the check — note that no escape square remains on the diagonal: the checking queen sweeps every one of them herself. The g2-pawn waits, one step from glory, a step it will never take.
The same queen's line that delivered the check now scoops up the pawn: g2 sits ON the a8-h1 diagonal. One check = one tempo = the whole race. What follows is the queen mate, taught in its own course.

The exact mirror of the main line: it is BLACK's promotion that lands with check — the white king put itself on the g1-a7 diagonal by playing Kb6. The "lost" tempo did not dissolve: it changed owners.
And the brand-new queen even affords the luxury of giving the material back: it buys the a7-pawn and the cleanest draw there is.
Two bare kings. The whole story of pawn races fits in this diptych: one tempo's difference, two diagonals — and the check decides, never the count alone.

Two pawns beat one — especially when one guards the other. A PROTECTED passed pawn isn't just an extra pawn: it's untouchable, and the weaker side can wear itself out approaching it, the result won't change.
Taking it only hastens the end
Even without taking it: lost all the same
The reflex: “I take what's there for the taking” — except the c4 pawn was only there to guard d5. Once it's gone, d5 runs alone, and Black's king has just wandered off for good.
Black's king merely approaches, without capturing right away — the nuance changes nothing: the moment White pushes d6, the c4 guard no longer needs protecting, and the same race starts over.
Remember the picture, not the line: a protected passed pawn isn't fought HAND TO HAND — you ignore it, play elsewhere, and it does the job alone when the moment comes.
He takes it eventually anyway — one tempo later, which only worsens his lag behind the d-pawn, already well ahead.

The most common mate in chess — and the most botched: one over-eager queen move is stalemate, and hours of play evaporate. The method fits in one image: the queen sits a KNIGHT'S MOVE from the enemy king, and almost never checks.
The knight's-move distance
The stalemate of zeal
No check! The queen takes the king in a knight's L and steals half the board from him: the 7th rank, the c-file, both diagonals. Every royal flight will be answered by the same L.
The king moved, the queen re-takes her L (e4-c5: one knight's jump). He hasn't escaped — he has moved into a smaller box.
The L again. The queen isn't chasing the king: she is shrinking his world.
The queen confines all by herself — so it is the KING's turn to come. A queen mate is always teamwork: she cages, he finishes.
The white king takes the key square. Careful: HERE is where the over-eager queen stalemates — see the other chapter.

“One more little squeeze…” — STALEMATE. Count the opponent's squares BEFORE squeezing: b1, b2, c2, d1 taken by the queen, d2 by the king. Zero squares. Hours of play, half a point. The golden rule: once the enemy king touches the edge, look for MATE, not more confinement.
Check AND mate — the first check of the entire ending, and it is the last move. Remember that ratio: one hundred percent of the checks were useful.

The queen ending par excellence: one extra pawn, an opponent who will live on checks alone. The race is not won by fleeing the checks but by sheltering from them: the king slips under an "umbrella" made of its own pawn and queen, while White's own checks earn the tempi for promotion. A textbook position (Müller & Lamprecht): White to move wins, Black to move draws — a single tempo separates the two worlds.
The umbrella, the escorted promotion, the liquidation
Sheltering before there is a roof

The pawn first — the fastest conversion by twelve moves (verified: two other moves also win, but in 32 and 65 moves). In a queen ending the passed pawn is the only argument: everything else is just managing the enemy checks.

Raising the umbrella BEFORE sending the pawn: it looks prudent, and it throws the win away (verified: the position drops back to a draw). The umbrella's roof is the pawn on h7 — while it sits on h5, the king is stepping out into the rain.
The best defence: the black king rushes over — a lone queen cannot deliver perpetual check, it needs its king to tighten the net.
The storm begins. Count Black's checks from here: there will be only two before the well runs dry.
The first canvas of the umbrella: the queen interposes on the g-file AND takes up guard beside the h7-pawn. One move, two jobs — the hallmark of good queen-ending moves.
The umbrella is open: pawn on h7 overhead, queen on g6 at the flank — the king is in the dry. Check every line into h6: all blocked or covered. THE picture to remember from this ending.
Not a single check left — the black queen falls back to the long diagonal, a last glance at h8, the promotion square.
Your turn: WHITE's checks, on the other hand, pay. Each one moves the queen towards its final post while stealing the tempo.
A second tempo-check, and look at the arrival square: f8 controls h8 along the rank. The promotion is now escorted — the black queen's b2-h8 diagonal will not be enough.
Two queens against one. All that remains is to weather the final volley of checks — with two interpositions available, it is a simple matter of technique.
The king walks back into shelter between its two queens — g6, h7, g8: every step stays under cover.
The new queen's first duty: interpose. An extra queen is an extra shield — Black's checks now wear out against material, no longer against the king.
The second interposition — and this one cannot be sidestepped: every line into g8 runs through a white queen.
The defence is down to its last gesture: winning one queen back.

…and one remains. Queen against bare king: the elementary mate, taught in its own course. Remember the three-part mechanism: the pawn runs, the king shelters under the umbrella, and WHITE's checks pay for the promotion.
The downpour, immediately — the e3-h6 diagonal is wide open, with no canvas to close it.

And the defence's most elegant move: not a check — a PIN. The h5-pawn is nailed against its own king, frozen for good; any king move to unpin walks back into the checks. The draw is sealed: an umbrella without a roof shelters no one.

The same ending as “Queen vs Pawn”… except the pawn stands on c2, and everything flips: this is a DRAW, provided you know the real resource — which is not the one of legend. The tablebase has surprises for both sides.
Promote to trade
The screw spins loose
The legend of the a1 corner
The stalemate exists — for them
White lines up in front of the pawn. Against a central pawn the endless screw would win — here, watch the antidote.
The “normal” attack: the queen comes from behind, as against the central pawn.
The king stays GLUED to his pawn, ready to recapture on c1. He is the bodyguard of the coming trade.
The white king rushes over — he will never make it in time.
THE resource, and it isn't stalemate: promote TO TRADE. The c-file is now empty, the white queen must take — and the black king recaptures. Only two kings will remain.
Declining the trade leaves queen versus queen: also a draw.
King versus king. Remember the duo that holds this draw: king glued to the pawn + promotion-trade the moment the queen nears c1.
The queen touches the promotion zone. Against a d-pawn Black would be lost. Here…

…the promotion-trade AGAIN — and it is the ONLY move that holds: everything else loses, including the famous Ka1 (next chapter). The d2-queen stands too close: she can neither decline the trade nor win it.

The book move: “into the corner, and Qxc2 is stalemate”. The tablebase is categorical: played HERE, it LOSES. Stalemate is only a resource if the opponent agrees to capture — and he won't, not like this.
The lethal detour: the queen goes VIA c1 — the very square the king gave up when he left b1.

If White GOBBLES the pawn… STALEMATE — a2, b1 and b2 all covered by the queen, and the king can't breathe. That is where the legend comes from: the trap is real, but it traps a CARELESS ATTACKER — it is no reliable defence.
And the pawn falls WITH CHECK: no stalemate anywhere. The gap between legend and truth was one tempo — the one Ka1 gave away.
Queen against bare king: see “The Queen Mate”.

You queened first; your opponent is ONE square from doing the same. The queen beats a central pawn — but not by rushing: with an endless-screw of checks that forces the enemy king in front of its pawn, stealing one tempo per turn of the spiral.
The endless screw
What if he queens?
King first? No.
The queen doesn't rush the pawn: she checks while CLOSING IN — every check lands her one square nearer, zigzagging.
“My king is four steps away, let's run.” One tempo too slow: the pawn queens, and queen versus queen is no longer a win. ALWAYS the screw first — only it freezes the pawn.
Always the check that gains a square.
No check this time: the queen eyes d1 FROM BEHIND. The black king has only one way to keep his pawn alive…
…and here is the key to the whole ending: this check forces the king IN FRONT of his own pawn.
The pawn is gagged by its own king: Black has no threat left. That ONE-tempo respite is all the screw produces — and all that is needed.
THE stolen tempo: the white king takes one step. Then the screw restarts — checks, king in front, one step. Count the steps you need: that is your margin.
The king walks in WITHOUT taking the pawn: yes, d2 may promote — so what? Watch what follows: promotion saves nothing, and ignoring it is the shortest road.
The desperado KNIGHT — genuinely the tablebase's best defence: a queen would be born dead (see the other chapter). The knight at least gives check… postponing matters by two moves.
The “natural” promotion… and the queen is born to die: one square, one move, one mate.
The knight flees, threatening… nothing at all.
The runaway is pinned mid-stride — and the net closes.
Mate, knight watching from the balcony. The endless screw, the king walking in, the desperado refuted: the complete method in twelve moves.
The brand-new queen watches, helpless: b2 was the only square that mattered. THAT is why the knight was the better defence.
A theoretical draw. The whole ending was decided by White's first move.

Without pawns, the queen usually wins against rook and bishop — by splitting them apart with long-distance checks until zugzwang. The defence: keep all three Black pieces bunched together, each protecting another — a triangle the queen alone can never crack.
The triangle holds
The king wanders off, the triangle breaks
A long-distance check — the usual method for trying to split Black's pieces apart.
Black's king stays glued to its rook and bishop — the king-rook-bishop triangle doesn't break. Verified draw: no White try the oracle tested from this crossroads ever did better.
